bibliography.abstract: Residential relocations can affect well-being and travel behaviour in ambiguous ways. This study conceptualises moving voluntariness as an explanatory variable leading to favourable outcomes for voluntary movers and less favourable outcomes for involuntary movers. Specifically, we expect that voluntary movers will change or maintain travel behaviour in line with previous attitudes due to higher control and that involuntary movers will adapt more strongly to their new built environment due to lower control levels. We test this using longitudinal panel survey data of individuals expecting (n=1,234) and later realising a move (n=411). Using a novel, subjective voluntariness measure, we find that voluntary movers show improved well-being (i.e. mental health, life satisfaction, residential satisfaction, place attachment), while involuntary movers show similar but non-significant changes. Neither group shows changed travel attitude-behaviour consistencies, suggesting that subjective voluntariness does not directly translate into distinct travel behaviour change pathways. However, involuntary movers showed consistently weaker car orientations and lower mobility needs fulfilment, hinting at stable differences in travel characteristics of mover groups. Despite similar demographics, involuntary movers report lower perceived control, earlier moving stages, and higher future-location uncertainty. Our suggested subjective measure provides different well-being and travel insights than previous objective approaches. We suggest conceptual and methodological refinements, e.g. in terms of dimensionality, time-variability, reliability, and possible relations to personality/trait variables.
bibliography.title: Forced or desired residential relocation? Moving voluntariness and its effects on well-being and travel behaviour

en.caveats: The findings are based on a relatively small post-move sample size of 411 respondents, and the study relies on self-reported subjective measures of voluntariness and well-being.
en.what: This study tracks individuals before (n=1,234) and after (n=411) a residential relocation using longitudinal panel survey data to analyze how the voluntariness of a move affects well-being and travel behavior. Using a new subjective measure of voluntariness, the researchers found that voluntary movers experienced significant improvements in mental health, life satisfaction, residential satisfaction, and place attachment, whereas involuntary movers showed non-significant changes. While subjective voluntariness did not directly alter travel attitude-behavior consistency, involuntary movers exhibited weaker car orientations and lower fulfillment of mobility needs.
en.why: It demonstrates that subjective perceptions of moving voluntariness, rather than traditional objective classifications, reveal distinct differences in post-move well-being and highlight how involuntary movers face persistent disadvantages in mobility satisfaction and perceived control.
